beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Varun, and this video is about turning a living optic nerve into data a machine can read. Before you can teach a machine to spot glaucoma, you have to answer a harder question first: what, exactly, do you feed it? For two thousand years, the inside of a living eye was a black box. Our project depended on a technology that finally cracked it open.

beats.narration_original: Before you can teach a machine to spot glaucoma, you have to answer a harder question first: what, exactly, do you feed it? For two thousand years, the inside of a living eye was a black box. Our project depended on a technology that finally cracked it open.
beats.intro_line: Hi, I'm Varun, and this video is about turning a living optic nerve into data a machine can read.

beats.narration_text: A nerve becomes data when you measure its thickness. OCT reads the layer beneath the surface, micron by micron — and that map is what our whole project runs on.

props.text:
A nerve becomes data when you measure its surface.
OCT reads the layer beneath — micron by micron.

beats.narration_text: The first glimpse came around eighteen fifty, when the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz built the ophthalmoscope — light and mirrors that let a doctor see the living optic nerve for the first time. Within a few years, surgeons spotted glaucoma's fingerprint: the centre of the nerve head hollowed out, cupped, like a crater.

props.artifactHeading: What a mirror and a lamp revealed
artifactLines: For the first time, a living optic nerve is visible
Within a few years: glaucoma's fingerprint — the cupped nerve head
But a picture of the surface is not a measurement

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶2 — THE TAUGHT CONCEPT: what OCT measures
beats.narration_text: But a picture of the surface isn't enough. Glaucoma destroys a specific tissue — the retinal nerve fibre layer, a sheet of nerve cables microns thick. To fight it, you must measure that layer. That's what optical coherence tomography does. It fires a beam of light into the eye and reads the faint echoes from each retinal layer, timing them against a reference beam. It's ultrasound's trick, but with light — which is why it resolves detail down to thousandths of a millimetre.

props.caption: Schematic RNFL thickness map. Redrawn (simplified) — not patient data.

beats.narration_text: The output is a thickness map: exactly how much nerve tissue survives, point by point across the eye. That map is our raw material. And specifically, we built on the Harvard Glaucoma Detection and Progression dataset — Harvard-G-D-P — released by the Harvard Ophthalmology A-I Lab: one thousand patients, each with an O-C-T nerve-fibre map, made public for researchers. A thousand real eyes, turned into data.

props.sparkLine: A thousand real eyes, turned into data.
props.caption: Harvard-GDP — Harvard Ophthalmology AI Lab. One dot per patient.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶4 — the limitation that shaped everything
beats.narration_text: One thousand, though, is a tiny number in the world of deep learning. Models that recognise everyday objects train on millions of examples. And that limitation shaped everything we did next.

props.command: A thousand labelled examples is a rounding error in deep learning. Show me what a model can still do when the labels run out long before the data does.
props.runningText: counting what we do not have…
output: one thousand patients is a very small dataset

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: a thousand labelled examples sounds like a lot — explain why it's almost nothing to a modern A-I, and what specifically goes wrong when a deep network trains on too few labels. Ask for the failure mode by name, not just the word overfitting. If the answer doesn't tell you what the model learns instead of the real signal, push back.

props.command: A thousand labelled examples sounds like a lot — why is it almost nothing to a modern AI? Name the specific failure mode, and tell me what the model learns INSTEAD of the real signal.

beats.narration_text: Turning a Nerve into Data. With barely any labels to learn from, we had to teach a model to teach itself. Next time — the classifier.
